coverage_note: Surveyed all 16 continuing questions, the node and link graph, the five genre interactions, emotion targets and the five phases. Set aside: pairings resting only on a shared Book 24 decision or similar wording.

possibilities.title: A ledger that counts hours makes care auditable
possibilities.possibility: The Ledger now records the hours each hand worked beside the mark, so draw can be read from it. Interpretation: the same record that would let a shared accounting of care bind also makes surveillance of the tally cheap, and could harden the Book 20 conversion from a stage into infrastructure. It sits against the gift practice, whose point is labour given without a count. Worth testing whether the hours field is what turns care from offered into owed, and whether a terrace refusing to write hours is the quietest form of plurality.
possibilities.significance: It links three undecided questions through a recorded ledger revision, not wording, and could give the cost of counting a concrete, scene-level object rather than only a policy choice.

evidence.note: Revised summary: the ledger records hours each hand worked beside the mark, so a count of the draw can be read straight from it.
From Book 20 draw is partly set by hands owed, so recorded hours would bear directly on draw.
Names surveillance of the tally as a failure mode of the care-counting alternative.
Labour given without a count: the practice an hours record would expose.

assumptions: The hours record can be read by more than its keeper.
Hours are checkable by someone other than the labourer.
counterevidence: The tally is recorded as care, not debt, and does not hold the water.
Alternative A already counts care; hours may add detail, not a new consequence.
possibilities.gains: Turns an abstract counting question into a record that scenes and households can handle.
possibilities.costs: Risks making belonging read as a labour rota, a risk gi_political_pastoral_constrains already names.
possibilities.next_investigation: Trace who may read the hours record from Book 20 to Book 30 and sketch one household's season under it.

possibilities.title: Cistern headroom decides which practice the Long Return needs
possibilities.possibility: Release can only lower the high cistern, never raise it. The counted Turn holds water back to protect the cistern from surfeit; the gift practice needs release at need. The Long Return is a surge that must be routed through the Gate. Interpretation: if headroom matters on arrival, the practice that looked hazardous in Book 15 may be the one that makes room, and the counted Turn's caution may leave none. Cistern capacity could invert which practice the finale vindicates and fix where a threshold is meaningful.
possibilities.significance: One unestablished physical fact is recorded as a dependency of Alternatives B and C, and it also bears on the surge route and the threshold, so settling its relation to the pulse may narrow several choices.

evidence.note: Release draws the cistern down and cannot raise it; the Book 15 surfeit rests on a construction assumption.
The counted practice holds water back to protect the high cistern.
The gift practice needs release at need for the lower channels.
The pulse needs a Gate schedule that routes it; the routing decides which channel takes the surge.
Cistern storage above tolerance is not established; Alternatives B and C depend on it.

assumptions: The pulse is a surplus the high cistern may need to receive, not only flow through the Gate.
The counted Turn's holding persists to Book 30.
counterevidence: The Book 15 surfeit is an unconfirmed construction assumption the author may reject.
The pulse may route only through lower channels, making cistern headroom irrelevant.
No capacity value is canon; any number would be invented.
possibilities.gains: Gives the finale a physical, non-institutional reason for choosing among A, B and C.
possibilities.costs: Could make the finale an engineering puzzle and shrink the epic into civics, the risk in gi_epic_political_tension.
possibilities.next_investigation: Decide only whether the cistern can hold more or less than a pulse, then test each alternative against that relation.

possibilities.title: Apparent responsiveness explained by changed behaviour, not intent
possibilities.possibility: The spring responds to the draw-return balance, not intention, yet the epic contract promises a commons that answers choices. The Old Hand engine records that a reading changes whether returns are recorded, hence the balance. Interpretation: each intermediate reading between Books 8 and 15 could be a staged test where belief changes behaviour and the spring seems to answer intent while balance still explains it. The ontology stays unpromised, and wonder comes from an ambiguity the reader can resolve either way.
possibilities.significance: It reconciles a recorded tension between the epic promise and the balance-only engine, and gives the unresolved intent question and the intermediate readings a shared job without settling the ontology.

evidence.note: The spring responds to balance rather than to any character's intention.
A reading changes whether returns are recorded and therefore the balance on the Source.
Governing quest is to understand a physical commons that answers choices.
Book 15 gives a partial answer; the full ontology is deliberately not promised.

assumptions: Readings before Book 15 can alter recorded behaviour on the terraces.
Intermediate states are wanted at all; that is itself undecided.
counterevidence: Staged ambiguity may promise more than the deliberately unpromised ontology allows.
Mystery is only tertiary; more staged readings may postpone revelation, as gi_mystery_epic_enables warns.
possibilities.gains: Keeps wonder without committing the world to a mind in the spring.
possibilities.costs: Needs careful staging so ambiguity reads as design, not evasion.
possibilities.next_investigation: List what each reading would change in recorded returns, and see whether Books 8 to 15 need one or two intermediate states.

possibilities.title: The lowland debt may arrive as water
possibilities.possibility: Wild water recurs: the lowest Lowfen terrace in Book 1, the declined share in Book 21, and the Long Return's routing. Meanwhile the Compact's purchased draw returns no labour. Imaginative step: the lowland's debt and the surge's route are one decision, so the Book 30 routing could answer what lowland towns owe Ammen, and what Ammen owes them, in physical form rather than contract. Whether the lowland receives, refuses or shares the surge would bear on the Compact's claim.
possibilities.significance: It would let a politically abstract settlement be felt as an earned, costly physical choice, matching the hope target that the cost stays visible.

evidence.note: Purchased shares draw without return labour.
Under B, purchased draw owes grain-labour to the rebuild.
The pulse must be routed through the Gate.
Declining runs water wild down the lowest Lowfen terrace, a physical cost not a villain's act.

assumptions: The lowland and the lower channels share a water path; this is not recorded.
The lowland towns could choose to accept part of the surge.
counterevidence: The lowland question may be answered in trade or kinship rather than water.
Making a flood the payment for a debt could read as punishment, against the physical-cost framing.
possibilities.gains: Ties three scattered questions to a single Book 30 scene.
possibilities.costs: Invents a lowland water geography and may overload the routing choice.
possibilities.next_investigation: Check whether anything recorded connects lowland towns to the channels the surge could take.
